![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14120025/assets/001487e4a94988a24d15702a18692e9deb2495a7cc7ec5c9f71b98fea13e0ce8.png)

The path $C_1$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(-2,0)$ to the point $O(0,0),$ and the path $C_2$ consists of a line segment from the point $O(0,0)$ to the point $B(1,1).$

Given that $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = -4,$ evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf{F}(x, y) = (2x-3y) \,\mathbf{i} + (2y-5x)\,\mathbf {j}$ and $C = C_1\cup C_2.$
question.worked_solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
\int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r}
+
 \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r}.
$$

We're given the value of the first integral, so we only need to work out the second.

The path $C_2$ is the line segment from $O$ to $B.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}(t) & =b+t(c-b) \\  & =⟨0,0⟩+t(⟨1,1⟩-⟨0,0⟩) \\  & =⟨t,t⟩ \\  & =t\,i+t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0 \lt t \lt 1.$ Along this segment, we have $x = t$ and $y = t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t)) & =(2x-3y)\,i+(2y-5x)\,j \\  & =(2t-3t)\,i+(2t-5t)\,j \\  & =-t\,i-3t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =(-t\,i-3t\,j)\cdot (i+j) \\  & =-t\cdot 1+(-3t)\cdot 1 \\  & =-4t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-4+{\int }_{0}^{1}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4+{\int }_{0}^{1}(-4t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4+[-2{t}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =-4+[-2+0] \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$
